paras: The whipping of Ben Brand, a Black man also called Ben Evans, took place at Salem, South Carolina, in August 1888, when a party of citizens whipped him and ordered him out of the county over an alleged offense in a white household. The Manning Times first reported that Brand had been found hanged under the heading "Lynch Law in Salem," and a wire brief carried a version of the hanging to papers as far away as Rhode Island. Three weeks later the Times printed its correspondent's finding that no hanging had occurred and that Brand had left for Sumter county.

According to the Manning Times, Brand went to a white man's house in the Salem neighborhood about three weeks before its 29 August issue and obtained permission to spend the night. The paper said that during the night he "attempted some undue liberties in the house," while its later correspondent described the charge as "grossly insulting a married white woman."

Brand was severely whipped for the alleged offense and ordered to leave the county. The first report, attributed only to what the paper had been "informed," added that the order carried a penalty of death and that Brand, having stayed, was found dead the previous week hanging from a tree limb near Douglass swamp. The paper's Bethlehem correspondent, writing on 5 September, gave a different account: the whipping was done publicly, in daytime, by "a party of unmasked citizens, white and colored," and Brand then left the county.

The correspondent said he had investigated the reported hanging "by Klu Klux" and found "no truth whatever in it." He was "reliably informed" that Brand was picking cotton on the Fulwood place in Sumter county. No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution for the whipping appears in the coverage.

The Manning Times' first item treated the reported hanging as the expected result of Brand's defiance, ending, "He didn't leave, and the result is as above given." A wire brief that ran in the Narragansett Herald on 8 September, the Abbeville Press and Banner on 12 September, the West Virginia Argus on 13 September and the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer on 14 September called Brand "a desperado" detected in a burglary who was "taken from his captors and hanged by a mob." The burglary charge and the seizure from captors appear in no local account.

On 19 September the Times corrected itself under the heading "Was not a Case of Lynching," printing its correspondent's letter in full. The correction emphasized that the whippers were unmasked and included colored citizens, and it did not criticize the whipping itself. No correction of the wire version was found in the papers that carried it, and no Black-press coverage survives for this period in the collection searched.

Three versions of Brand's fate circulated: found hanged near Douglass swamp (Manning Times, 29 August), hanged by a mob after being taken from captors (wire brief), and alive in Sumter county after a whipping (Manning Times, 19 September). The last is the later account and rests on a local correspondent's stated investigation, whereas the first was explicitly secondhand.

reader.title: Whipping of Ben Brand
bases: The later local account says Brand was publicly whipped by a party of citizens and ordered out of the county, not killed (A6); the earlier hanging reports (A1, A3) were retracted by the paper that first printed one.

The Manning Times first reported on hearsay that Brand was found hanged (A1) and a wire brief said a mob hanged him (A3), but the same paper then printed its correspondent's investigation finding he was whipped, left the county and was alive in Sumter county (A6). The whipping was extralegal punishment for an alleged offense, but no killing is supported by the investigated account.

The hanging reported in A1 and the wire brief (A2-A5) is directly denied by the later, investigated report in the same paper (A6); all accounts agree only that Brand was accused and punished at Salem.

accounts.label: Manning Times first report (hearsay)
accounts.gist: Brand was whipped and ordered to leave on pain of death for 'undue liberties' in a white man's house; he stayed and was found dead hanging from a tree near Douglass swamp.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: Brand, 'a desperado' detected in a burglary at Salem, was taken from his captors and hanged by a mob.

accounts.label: Bethlehem correspondent's investigation
accounts.gist: There was no hanging; Brand, alias Evans, was publicly whipped in daytime by unmasked white and colored citizens for insulting a married white woman, ordered out, and left for Sumter county.

framing.detail: The Manning Times' 'Lynch Law in Salem' presented the hanging as the consequence of Brand's failure to obey the order to leave: 'He didn't leave, and the result is as above given.'
The wire brief, run in South Carolina, North Carolina, West Virginia and Rhode Island news columns, called Brand 'a desperado' and gave the burglary version.

The follow-up 'Was not a Case of Lynching' denied the Klan hanging and stressed the whippers were unmasked and included colored citizens, while presenting the whipping for 'grossly insulting a married white woman' without criticism.
